title: Escrow Shortage: Why Your Mortgage Payment Went Up
description: Got an escrow shortage notice? Learn why your mortgage payment went up, how the annual escrow analysis works, and what California homeowners should check.
keywords: why did my mortgage payment go up
image_alt: A calculator, house keys on a keychain and a small model house resting on a table with financial documents

faq.q: Why did my mortgage payment go up if I have a fixed-rate loan?
faq.a: On a fixed-rate loan, principal and interest stay the same, but the escrow portion can change. If your property taxes or homeowners insurance premium went up, your servicer raises the escrow deposit to cover them.

An escrow shortage means your account is projected to have less than it needs to pay upcoming tax and insurance bills. Servicers typically let you repay it over the next year's payments or in a lump sum.

faq.q: Can I pay my escrow shortage all at once?
faq.a: Many servicers allow it. A lump-sum payment removes the catch-up portion from your monthly payment, but any increase from higher ongoing taxes or insurance still applies.

faq.q: Can I remove escrow from my mortgage?
faq.a: It depends on your loan type, your servicer's policies and often your equity. Some loans require escrow for the life of the loan. Ask your servicer what applies to yours.

body_html:
The envelope from your loan servicer looks routine. Then you read it: your monthly mortgage payment is going up next year, and there's a line that says "escrow shortage." You have a fixed-rate loan. You haven't missed a payment. So what happened?

This is one of the most common calls homeowners make after their first year or two in a home, and late in the year is when a lot of these notices land. The good news is that an escrow increase almost never means anything is wrong with your loan. It means the bills your servicer pays on your behalf changed. Once you understand how the annual escrow analysis works, the notice gets a lot less scary, and you'll know exactly which questions to ask.

What Your Escrow Account Actually Pays

If your loan has an escrow account (often called an impound account here in California), your monthly payment has two jobs. Part of it pays your loan: principal and interest. The other part goes into a holding account your servicer uses to pay your property taxes and homeowners insurance when those bills come due. Some homeowners also have flood insurance or mortgage insurance in the mix.

Here's the key point: on a fixed-rate loan, the principal and interest portion doesn't change. The escrow portion can. Your county sets your taxes and your insurer sets your premium. Your servicer is just passing those costs through, spread across twelve monthly payments.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau lists escrow changes first among the reasons a monthly mortgage payment can go up, noting that it happens when property taxes or homeowners insurance premiums change (CFPB).

How the Annual Escrow Analysis Works

Once a year, your servicer reviews the account. It looks back at what it actually paid out over the past year, then projects what it expects to pay over the next twelve months. That review is called an escrow analysis, and you'll receive a statement summarizing it. Federal rules under the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (Regulation X, section 1024.17) govern how servicers run these accounts, including how much of a cushion they can hold and what happens when there's too much or too little in the account.

The analysis can land in one of three places:

  • Balanced: what came in matched what went out, and next year's projection looks similar. Your escrow payment stays about the same.
  • Surplus: the account collected more than it needed, often because a tax bill or premium came in lower than expected. Depending on the amount and whether your loan is current, you may receive a refund or see a lower payment.
  • Shortage: the account is projected to run short, usually because taxes or insurance went up. Your payment rises to cover the higher ongoing cost, and there may be a catch-up amount on top of that.

A shortage notice often contains two increases rolled together, and they're worth separating.

Shortage vs. Higher Ongoing Costs

When your escrow payment goes up after a shortage, it's usually a combination of these two pieces:

PieceWhat it isIs it permanent?
New baselineYour taxes or insurance now cost more each year, so the monthly escrow deposit has to rise to match.Yes, until those bills change again.
Shortage catch-upLast year's deposits didn't cover last year's bills, so the account needs to be refilled.No. It's a one-time gap, typically spread across the next year's payments or paid in a lump sum.

This distinction matters because it changes how you plan. If most of your increase is the catch-up, your payment may ease back somewhat after a year, assuming your bills hold steady. If most of it is the new baseline, that's your new normal.

Many servicers let you pay the shortage in a lump sum instead of spreading it out. Doing so removes the catch-up portion from your monthly payment, though the new baseline still applies. Your escrow statement should spell out the options your servicer offers. If it isn't clear, call and ask.

Why Southern California Homeowners See This So Often

A few local factors make escrow changes more common here than people expect.

Your taxes may have reset after you bought. In California, a home's assessed value generally resets to the purchase price when it changes hands. If your escrow account was set up using the previous owner's lower tax figures, the first full year of taxes at your new value can create a shortage. I covered the related one-time bill in Supplemental Property Tax Bills: A California Buyer's Guide. That supplemental bill is a separate issue, but it comes from the same reassessment, and it's a good signal to check whether your escrow account was sized for your new value.

Insurance premiums have been moving. The California homeowners insurance market has been under real pressure, and renewals can come in higher than the year before. Some homeowners have also changed carriers or ended up on the FAIR Plan with a separate policy for gaps in coverage. Any of these can change what your servicer pays out. If you want the bigger picture, see California Homeowners Insurance: What Buyers Need to Know Now.

Special assessments and Mello-Roos. Many newer Orange County and Inland Empire communities carry special taxes that appear on the property tax bill. Those amounts can change, and they flow through your escrow just like the base tax.

What to Check When the Notice Arrives

Don't just accept the new number, and don't panic over it either. Spend fifteen minutes with the statement and look for these things:

  1. Compare the tax figure to your actual tax bill. Your county's online tax lookup will show what was billed. If the servicer's projection doesn't match, ask why.
  2. Compare the insurance figure to your current declarations page. A servicer may still be projecting an old premium or a policy you've since replaced.
  3. Look for exemptions that weren't applied. California's homeowners' exemption has to be filed with your county assessor. If you haven't filed, ask your assessor's office about it.
  4. Check for double payments. If you paid a tax installment yourself and the servicer also paid it, the county may issue a refund, and the account math can get tangled. Sort it out with your servicer.
  5. Confirm it's actually escrow. The CFPB notes other reasons a payment can change, including the end of a temporary buydown, an adjustable rate resetting, mortgage insurance changes, new fees, or a servicer error. Read the breakdown line by line.

If you believe there's a mistake, the CFPB recommends contacting your servicer first, and if that doesn't resolve it, sending a written notice of error to the servicer's designated address. Keep notes of who you spoke with and when.

Should You Get Rid of Your Escrow Account?

Some homeowners respond to a shortage notice by asking to drop escrow and pay taxes and insurance themselves. Whether that's possible depends on your loan type, your servicer's policies, and often how much equity you have. Some loans require escrow for the life of the loan.

Even when it's allowed, think it through. Without escrow, you'll face large property tax installments twice a year and an annual insurance premium on your own schedule. That works well for disciplined savers. For others, the monthly structure is what keeps a big bill from becoming a crisis. An escrow shortage is a symptom of higher costs, not a flaw in escrow itself. Paying the bills directly doesn't make them any smaller.

If tax questions come up, such as whether you qualify for an exemption or how payments affect your return, talk to a tax professional. I'm happy to help you read the mortgage side of the statement.

The Takeaway

An escrow shortage notice isn't a penalty and it isn't a sign your loan changed. It's your servicer adjusting to what your taxes and insurance actually cost now. Separate the new baseline from the one-time catch-up, check the numbers against your real tax bill and insurance declarations, and ask questions if something doesn't line up.

And if a rising payment has you wondering whether your overall loan setup still fits your budget, that's a good conversation to have. Reach out and I'll walk through your statement with you and talk about what options might make sense for your situation.
